title: Data That Belongs to Everyone
subject: AI-Literacy
description: How shared, open data helps people solve real problems: reading an AQI table, the 2020 Covid dip, the Delhi smog investigation, one dataset serving many users, combining datasets, building your own dataset report, benefits and concerns of open data, and the WHO Global Air Quality Database.

questions.question: In this chapter, what does 'open data' mean?
options: Information anyone can freely use and share
Information kept secret by one company
Information stored only in paper files
Information that costs money to look at
questions.explanation: The chapter calls it 'data that belongs to everyone' — facts that are free and public so anyone can use and share them, like the air data the reporters used.

questions.question: Open data is called 'data that belongs to everyone' because it is free for all to use.
questions.explanation: That is exactly the idea in the title: the air data was public and free, so reporters, doctors and governments could all use it.

questions.question: The big question at the top of the worksheet asks how shared data can help people do what?
questions.explanation: The worksheet opens with: 'How can shared data help people solve real problems?' Every activity after that answers this question.

questions.question: Why could the reporters share their pollution findings so easily?
options: The government ordered them to share
They kept the data in a secret file
The data they used was free and public
They paid a company to release it
questions.explanation: The worksheet says 'Because the data was free, they could share their work easily.' Open data has no locks or fees, so findings built on it can be passed around.

questions.question: Open data can only be used by the government that collected it.
questions.explanation: False. The whole point of open data is that it is NOT limited to its collector — reporters, doctors, principals and AI researchers all used the same government air data.

questions.question: Which of these is the best example of open data from the chapter?
options: A diary a student keeps locked at home
A password written on a sticky note
A secret recipe kept by a restaurant
Air quality numbers published by the CPCB
questions.explanation: CPCB Open Data (cpcb.nic.in) is named as a source — the government publishes air readings for anyone to use. Diaries, passwords and secret recipes are private, not open.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements that describe open data as the chapter uses the term.
options: It can be shared with others
questions.explanation: Open data is free and shareable. If only experts could see it, or if it had to be bought, it would not 'belong to everyone'.

questions.question: Which statement about open data is NOT true?
options: It can only be used for one purpose
It is free for the public to use
It can be combined with other data
It can help people make decisions
questions.explanation: The worksheet shows the SAME AQI dataset used for many different purposes (news, health, school, AI). So 'only one purpose' is the false statement; the other three are all shown in the chapter.

questions.question: In the chapter, who 'owns' data that belongs to everyone?
options: Only the scientists who study it
Everyone who wants to use it
Only the person who typed it
Only the company that stores it
questions.explanation: The title says the data belongs to Everyone. Nobody has to ask permission from a typist, a company or a scientist to use open data.

questions.question: The CPCB open data website address given in the worksheet is which of these?
questions.explanation: The worksheet lists 'CPCB Open Data — cpcb.nic.in'. The '.nic.in' ending is used by Indian government websites.

questions.question: What is the opposite of open data?
options: Data printed in a big newspaper
Data shown on a public website
Data shared at a school meeting
Data locked away so few can see it
questions.explanation: Open data is free and visible to all. Its opposite is data that is locked or hidden. Newspapers, public websites and school meetings all SHARE data, so they are examples of openness.

questions.question: A city posts its daily air readings on a free website. A factory keeps its smoke readings in a private file. Which is open data?
options: Neither set, since both are numbers
questions.explanation: Open data must be free and available to everyone. The city's website readings are; the factory's private file is not. Being 'numbers' does not make data open or closed — access does.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that make a dataset 'open' in the chapter's sense.
questions.explanation: Openness is about ACCESS: anyone may use it, for free. The topic (air), the tool (Canva) and the number of columns do not decide whether data is open.

questions.question: 'Public data' in the Delhi story means data that...
options: Was voted for by the public in a poll
Is available to the public, not just officials
Was collected by the public themselves
Is about the public's favourite foods
questions.explanation: 'Free public data' means the government made its air readings available to everybody, not only to officials. It does not mean ordinary people collected it or voted on it.

questions.question: What does AQI stand for?
questions.explanation: AQI is the Air Quality Index — a number scale that tells how clean or polluted the air is.

questions.question: In Q1, where on the dataset was the AQI scale shown?
options: At the top of the dataset
questions.explanation: Q1 says 'Look at the AQI scale at the top of the dataset' — you use that scale to turn each city's number into a category.

questions.question: On the AQI scale, what does a HIGHER number mean?
questions.explanation: AQI measures pollution: the higher the number, the dirtier the air. It does not measure temperature or city size.

questions.question: Q1 asked students to fill each city's 2022 AQI category in which part of the table?
questions.explanation: Q1 says to fill 'each city's 2022 AQI category in the last column of the table'.

questions.question: The city with the highest AQI number had the worst air quality.
questions.explanation: True. Higher AQI = more pollution, so the highest number marks the worst air. That is how you answer Q1(a).

questions.question: A low AQI number means a city has dangerous, dirty air.
questions.explanation: False — it is the other way round. LOW AQI means cleaner, safer air; HIGH AQI means dirty air.

questions.question: To find the city with the BEST air quality in 2022, what should you look for?
options: The city with the most people
The city nearest to the sea
The lowest AQI number in that year
The highest AQI number in that year
questions.explanation: Best air = least pollution = lowest AQI. Q1(b) is answered by scanning the 2022 column for the smallest number, not by population or location.

questions.question: Aman's city has an AQI of 160 and Bela's city has an AQI of 55. Who breathes cleaner air?
options: Both the same, both are numbers
Neither, AQI is not about air
questions.explanation: Lower AQI means cleaner air, so Bela's 55 is better than Aman's 160. A bigger number is NOT better on this scale.

questions.question: An AQI 'category' tells you what about a city's number?
options: The band it falls in, such as good or poor
The name of the city that measured it
The year when the reading was taken
The scientist who wrote the number
questions.explanation: The scale at the top of the dataset groups numbers into categories (bands) like good, moderate or poor. Q1 asks you to write the matching band for each city.

questions.question: Select ALL the things the AQI table in Q1 contained.
questions.explanation: Q1 talks about 'each city' and compares 2020 with 'the other years', so the table had many cities and many years. Hospital bills and farmers' names belong to Q2's story, not the table.

questions.question: Which year's data in the table 'looked different from the other years'?
questions.explanation: Q1(c) says 'The 2020 data looks different from the other years' and explains that 2020 was the Covid-19 pandemic year.

questions.question: If a city's AQI category changes from 'good' to 'very poor', what most likely happened?
questions.explanation: AQI categories track pollution. Moving to a worse band means the air got dirtier. Population, rain or roads are not what AQI measures.

questions.question: Comparing cities on the AQI table is an example of using data to do what?
questions.explanation: Because every city is measured on the same AQI scale, the table lets you compare them fairly — which Q1(a) and Q1(b) ask you to do.

questions.question: Why is a shared scale like AQI useful when comparing many cities?
options: Every city is measured the same way
Every city gets the same number
Every city must build a factory
questions.explanation: A shared scale means one rule for everyone, so numbers from different cities can be compared honestly. It does not make the numbers equal.

questions.question: An AQI table with cities as rows and years as columns lets you compare which two things?
options: Cities with each other and years over time
Hospitals with schools across a city
questions.explanation: Reading down a column compares cities in one year; reading across a row shows how one city changed over the years — both are used in Q1.

questions.question: In Q1(a) you are asked which city had the WORST air quality in which year?
questions.explanation: Q1(a) asks: 'Which city had the worst air quality in 2022?' — the same year whose categories you fill in the last column.

questions.question: What happened in 2020 that made the AQI data look different?
questions.explanation: Q1(c) says '2020 was when the Covid-19 pandemic happened', which explains why the 2020 numbers stand out.

questions.question: Why did the AQI improve for ALL cities during 2020?
options: Lockdowns kept cars and factories mostly stopped
Every city planted millions of new trees
Strong winds blew the pollution to the sea
The AQI scale was changed to a new one
questions.explanation: During the pandemic people stayed home, so traffic and many factories stopped. Less burning of fuel means less smoke, so the air got cleaner everywhere at once.

questions.question: During 2020 the AQI of the cities improved, meaning the air got cleaner.
questions.explanation: True. 'Improved' AQI means lower numbers and cleaner air — the pandemic lockdowns cut pollution.

questions.question: In 2020 the air in the cities became dirtier than in other years.
questions.explanation: False. The worksheet says the AQI IMPROVED in 2020 — the air was cleaner, not dirtier, because of lockdowns.

questions.question: During the pandemic, fewer vehicles were on the roads. What effect did that have on the air?
options: More rain fell on the city
No change in the air at all
questions.explanation: Vehicles burn fuel and release smoke. Fewer vehicles means less smoke, which is why the AQI improved in 2020.

questions.question: Which is the best explanation of the 2020 data, using the worksheet's hint?
options: Farmers burned more crops than usual that year
The government deleted the bad readings in 2020
People stayed home, so less pollution was made
Measuring machines broke, so numbers were wrong
questions.explanation: The hint is the Covid-19 pandemic: lockdowns kept people home, so less pollution was produced. The other options invent problems the worksheet never mentions.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that were likely reduced during the 2020 lockdowns.
questions.explanation: Lockdowns cut traffic and factory activity — the two big sources of city air pollution. The number of cities and hospitals did not shrink.

questions.question: What does the 2020 dip teach us about air pollution?
options: It is caused only by the weather outside
It can never be reduced by anyone
It only ever happens in the winter
Much of it comes from human activity
questions.explanation: When human activity (traffic, factories) paused, the air got cleaner. That shows people cause much of the pollution — and that it CAN be reduced.

questions.question: In Q1(c), the AQI numbers of which cities improved in 2020?
options: All the cities in the table
questions.explanation: Q1(c)(i) asks 'Why did the AQI improve for ALL cities during 2020?' — the change showed up everywhere, not in one city.

questions.question: After the lockdowns ended, what would you EXPECT the AQI numbers to do?
options: Drop to exactly zero at once
questions.explanation: The 2020 improvement came from reduced activity. When cars and factories restarted, pollution — and AQI — would be expected to climb back up.

questions.question: Noticing that one year 'looks different' in a table is called spotting a what?
questions.explanation: Q1(c) trains you to look at numbers across years and notice when the pattern breaks — the 2020 dip is a pattern change.

questions.question: Which data would best CONFIRM the lockdown explanation for the 2020 dip?
options: A list of popular songs in 2020
The number of schools in each city
Traffic counts showing far fewer cars
questions.explanation: If traffic counts fell sharply in 2020 while AQI improved, that supports the idea that fewer vehicles cleaned the air. Songs, school counts and cricket scores are unrelated.

questions.question: Who caused the AQI to improve in 2020, whether they meant to or not?
options: Only the farmers, by burning less
Only the doctors, by treating more
Only the reporters, by writing more
questions.explanation: The improvement was city-wide and in every city, because nearly everyone stopped travelling and many workplaces closed — not because of one small group.

questions.question: Between which years did reporters study air pollution in the worksheet's story?
questions.explanation: Q2 begins: 'Between 2018 and 2021, reporters used free public data, hospital notes, and satellite pictures to study air pollution.'

questions.question: Select ALL the kinds of information the reporters used, besides free public data.
questions.explanation: The reporters combined free public data with hospital notes and satellite pictures. Tickets, report cards and scores were not part of the study.

questions.question: What caused Delhi's WORST smog, according to the reporters?
questions.explanation: The reporters found 'Delhi's worst smog happened when nearby farmers burned crops'. Smoke from the burning fields drifted over the city.

questions.question: What happened to hospital visits when the air got dirty?
options: They dropped because people stayed in
They rose only for broken bones
questions.explanation: The worksheet says 'Dirty air caused a jump in hospital visits for breathing problems.' Polluted air hurts the lungs, so more people needed help.

questions.question: The reporters used satellite pictures as one of their data sources.
questions.explanation: True — satellite pictures (along with free public data and hospital notes) are listed in Q2.

questions.question: The reporters found that Delhi's worst smog was caused by ocean winds.
questions.explanation: False. The cause they found was nearby farmers burning crops, not winds from the sea.

questions.question: How did the government use the reporters' work?
options: To help make new clean-air rules
To build a new airport runway
To plan a bigger cricket stadium
questions.explanation: Q2 ends: 'the government used it to help make new clean-air rules.' The data led to real action against pollution.

questions.question: Why could the reporters share their work easily?
options: Because they owned a TV channel
questions.explanation: The worksheet gives the reason directly: 'Because the data was free, they could share their work easily.'

questions.question: Put the chain in order: ? → dirty air → more hospital visits. What goes in the first blank?
questions.explanation: Crop burning made the smog, the smog dirtied the air, and the dirty air sent people to hospital. Rules, sharing and pictures came AFTER, not before.

questions.question: Dirty air in Delhi led to a jump in hospital visits for breathing problems.
questions.explanation: True — that was one of the reporters' key findings in Q2.

questions.question: Which news source is named for the Delhi smog study?
questions.explanation: The source line reads 'IndiaSpend — indiaspend.com/...stubble-burning-the-main-culprit-behind-delhis-worsening-air-quality'.

questions.question: Select ALL the things that happened BECAUSE the data was free.
options: The government could use it for rules
Hospitals closed down for a year
Reporters could share their work easily
questions.explanation: Free data meant the reporters' work could spread easily, and the government could pick it up to make clean-air rules. Farmers and hospitals did not shut down.

questions.question: Which statement about the Delhi study is NOT true?
questions.explanation: The reporters used FREE public data — nothing was paid for or secret. The other three statements are all taken directly from Q2.

questions.question: What did the hospital notes most likely show the reporters?
options: How many rules the government wrote
How many people came in with breathing trouble
How many farmers lived near the city
How many satellites passed over Delhi
questions.explanation: Hospital notes record patients and their problems, so they revealed the jump in breathing-problem visits on smoggy days.

questions.question: What did the satellite pictures most likely show?
options: The price of vegetables in markets
The timetable of trains to Delhi
Smoke from fields where crops were burned
The names of patients in hospitals
questions.explanation: Satellites look down from space, so they can show smoke rising from burning fields near Delhi — evidence linking crop burning to the smog.

questions.question: What is 'smog'?
options: A light morning fog after rain
A warm wind from the desert
A cloud that brings heavy snow
Dirty, smoky air hanging over a city
questions.explanation: Smog is smoke mixed with fog — thick, dirty air that sits over a city. In Delhi it came from burning crops.

questions.question: The Delhi story shows that open data can lead to what final result?
options: Real changes in laws and rules
Nothing, since data is just numbers
questions.explanation: The chain ended with the government using the findings 'to help make new clean-air rules' — open data changed real policy, not just headlines.

questions.question: The Delhi smog study appears in which worksheet level?
questions.explanation: Q2 (the Delhi story and the two tables) sits under the 'Powering up' level, after 'Laying the tracks' (Q1).

questions.question: In the Delhi story, which event came LAST?
questions.explanation: Order: farmers burned crops → smog → hospital visits rose → reporters shared findings → the government made clean-air rules. The rules were the final step.

questions.question: Q2(a) says different people use the same open dataset for what?
questions.explanation: Q2(a) reads: 'Different people use the same open dataset for completely different purposes.' One table, many uses.

questions.question: A JOURNALIST would most likely use AQI data to do what?
options: Write a news report about dirty air
Train a computer to predict smog
questions.explanation: Journalists report news. With AQI data they can show readers how bad the air is — just like the IndiaSpend reporters did.

questions.question: A PUBLIC HEALTH DOCTOR might use AQI data to decide what?
options: Which pattern a computer should learn
When to warn patients about dirty air
Which day to hold the school fair
questions.explanation: Doctors care for health. High AQI days are risky for people with breathing problems, so the doctor can warn them in time.

questions.question: A SCHOOL PRINCIPAL might use AQI data to decide what?
options: Which medicine to prescribe to patients
Which data to feed into a computer model
Whether to keep children indoors at break
Which story to publish in the paper
questions.explanation: A principal is responsible for pupils' safety. On a very-poor AQI day, keeping children indoors protects their lungs.

questions.question: An AI RESEARCHER might use AQI data to do what?
options: Plan the school's outdoor sports day
Train a model to predict pollution
questions.explanation: AI researchers teach computers with data. Years of AQI readings can train a model to forecast smoggy days.

questions.question: Select ALL the groups listed in the Q2(a) table of data users.
questions.explanation: The table lists four users: Journalist, Public health doctor, School principal and AI researcher. Drivers, shopkeepers and pilots are not in it.

questions.question: A school principal was one of the data users listed in the worksheet.
questions.explanation: True — the Q2(a) table includes a School principal alongside a journalist, a public health doctor and an AI researcher.

questions.question: The worksheet listed a farmer as one of the four users of AQI data.
questions.explanation: False. Farmers appear in the Delhi story as the source of crop smoke, but the four users in the table are journalist, doctor, principal and AI researcher.

questions.question: 'Should I cancel the outdoor sports day because of the smog?' Who in the Q2(a) table asks this?
questions.explanation: Sports day is a school decision, so it is the principal's question. The journalist reports, the doctor treats, the researcher builds models.

questions.question: 'Can a computer learn to predict next week's smog?' Who in the Q2(a) table asks this?
questions.explanation: Teaching a computer to predict is the AI researcher's job. The others use AQI data to act, not to build models.

questions.question: 'Should I tell my asthma patients to stay inside today?' Who in the Q2(a) table asks this?
questions.explanation: Advising patients is the public health doctor's decision. A principal advises pupils, not patients.

questions.question: Why is it powerful that ONE dataset serves many users?
options: Each user must collect fresh numbers
Only one person is allowed to read it
The numbers change for every user
One set of numbers helps many decisions
questions.explanation: Because the data is open, it is collected once and reused by everyone — journalists, doctors, principals and researchers each make their own decisions from it.

questions.question: Which is NOT a sensible use of AQI data from the Q2(a) table?
options: Choosing the colour of the school uniform
Deciding whether to warn breathing patients
Writing a report on a city's dirty air
Training a model to forecast pollution
questions.explanation: AQI tells you about air quality. It can guide health warnings, news reports and pollution forecasts, but it says nothing about uniform colours.

questions.question: The Q2(a) table asked for 'the specific ___ this data helps them make'.
questions.explanation: The column heading is 'The specific decision this data helps them make' — each user turns the data into a choice.

questions.question: A bus company starts using the AQI dataset to plan extra buses on smoggy days. What does this show about open data?
options: It must be re-collected for each new user
It loses value when more people use it
It can serve users nobody planned for
It works only for the four listed users
questions.explanation: The worksheet's four users are just examples. Because the data is open, any new group — like a bus company — can pick it up and make its own decision.

questions.question: Why did the worksheet ask about FOUR different users instead of just one?
options: To make the table look longer
To test spelling of job names
To prove only one user matters
To show one dataset has many uses
questions.explanation: Listing a journalist, doctor, principal and AI researcher shows how one open dataset can power very different decisions.

questions.question: The worksheet's example in Q2(b) combined AQI data with which other data?
questions.explanation: Q2(b) gives the example 'AQI with hospital to know if AQI leads to breathing problems'.

questions.question: Combining AQI data with hospital data helps people find out what?
options: Whether the city has enough green parks
Whether dirty air causes breathing problems
Whether hospitals have enough spare beds
Whether doctors enjoy working at night
questions.explanation: If hospital visits for breathing trouble rise on high-AQI days, that links dirty air to breathing problems — exactly what Q2(b)'s example says.

questions.question: What is the main idea of Q2(b)?
options: AQI data is useless on its own
questions.explanation: Q2(b) says 'People can combine AQI data with other datasets to learn new things.' Combining is how you discover links one table cannot show.

questions.question: You combine AQI data with SCHOOL ATTENDANCE data. What could you learn?
options: Which teacher is the most popular
How many desks each classroom has
Which subject students like the most
Whether dirty-air days keep children home
questions.explanation: Matching smoggy days with absence numbers could show whether pollution keeps pupils away. Teachers, desks and favourite subjects have nothing to do with AQI.

questions.question: You combine AQI data with TRAFFIC COUNT data. What could you learn?
options: Whether more cars mean worse air
Which car colour is most common
How long a traffic light stays red
Which road has the most potholes
questions.explanation: If AQI rises on days with heavy traffic, that suggests vehicles are a cause of pollution — a new finding from joining the two tables.

questions.question: You combine AQI data with WIND and WEATHER data. What could you learn?
options: Which city has the tallest buildings
How weather moves or traps pollution
How many umbrellas a shop sells
Which month has the longest days
questions.explanation: Wind can blow smoke away or hold it over a city. Pairing weather with AQI shows when and why pollution builds up.

questions.question: Select ALL the datasets that would sensibly pair with AQI data to learn about HEALTH.
questions.explanation: Hospital visits and asthma medicine sales both reflect breathing health, so they can reveal links with dirty air. Ice-cream and library data cannot.

questions.question: Joining two datasets can show a link that one dataset alone cannot.
questions.explanation: True — AQI alone shows air quality; hospital data alone shows illness; together they can show that one leads to the other.

questions.question: Data can only be useful when it is kept separate from other data.
questions.explanation: False. Q2(b) and the Delhi study show the opposite: combining datasets (AQI + hospital notes + satellite pictures) is what uncovered the cause.

questions.question: When two datasets are combined, what must they share so their rows can be matched?
options: The same person who typed them
The same number of pages printed
The same place and time, like city and year
The same colour of table heading
questions.explanation: To link AQI with hospital visits you match the SAME city on the SAME day or year. Headings, typists and page counts do not matter.

questions.question: AQI goes up on the same days that hospital visits go up. What is the careful conclusion?
options: Hospitals cause the air to get dirty
The numbers are a coincidence for sure
Nothing can be learned from two tables
The two seem linked and worth studying
questions.explanation: Rising together suggests a link — in Delhi it turned out dirty air caused the visits. Jumping to 'hospitals cause smog' reverses cause and effect.

questions.question: The worksheet says AQI data can only be combined with hospital data.
questions.explanation: False. Hospital data is just the example given; Q2(b) then asks YOU to suggest two other datasets to combine with AQI.

questions.question: Q2(b) asked students to write how many combination ideas?
questions.explanation: The Q2(b) table has two numbered rows (1. and 2.) for students' own combination ideas.

questions.question: Q2(b)'s second column asks: 'What new thing could this help people ___?'
questions.explanation: The column heading is 'What new thing could this help people find out?' — combining data is about discovering something new.

questions.question: You combine AQI data with the dates farmers burn crops. What could you check?
options: Whether crops grow taller in summer
Whether tractors cost more each year
Whether burning days match smog days
Whether farmers like the colour red
questions.explanation: This is what the Delhi reporters effectively did — matching crop-burning dates with bad-air days showed that burning caused the smog.

questions.question: The Delhi reporters' work is an example of combining datasets.
questions.explanation: True — they joined air data, hospital notes and satellite pictures, which is exactly the skill Q2(b) asks about.

questions.question: Select ALL the NEW things that combining datasets can reveal that one table alone could not.
options: The title of the hospital table
A link between two kinds of events
A cause that one table alone hid
The AQI number for one city
questions.explanation: Combining is for finding links and causes (dirty air → breathing problems). A single city's AQI or a table title is already visible in one table.

questions.question: Why did the worksheet give 'AQI with hospital data' as the first example?
options: To show hospitals own the AQI data
To prove AQI data is always wrong
To list every hospital in the city
To model how combining reveals links
questions.explanation: The example shows the pattern — pair AQI with another dataset to learn something new — so students can invent their own pairs in rows 1 and 2.

questions.question: Q3 asked students to create a dataset report about something useful where?
options: A faraway country they have never seen
The surface of the Moon or Mars
A made-up land from a storybook
questions.explanation: Q3 says the report should be 'about something useful in your school, neighbourhood, or city' — real, nearby data.

questions.question: Select ALL the tools the worksheet suggested for making the report.
questions.explanation: Q3 names Canva, Google Slides or a spreadsheet as digital tools for the report.

questions.question: How many columns must the Q3 table have?
questions.explanation: Q3 requires 'a table with 5 columns and 3 rows of data'.

questions.question: How many rows of data must the Q3 table have?
questions.explanation: Q3 requires 5 columns and 3 rows of data — don't swap them!

questions.question: Q3 says one column must include what?
options: A map, like a city plan
questions.explanation: Q3: 'Include one column with a scale (example: noise level, temperature, cleanliness rating)'.

questions.question: Select ALL the scale examples that Q3 named.
questions.explanation: The worksheet's examples of a scale column are noise level, temperature and cleanliness rating.

questions.question: The topic you choose for Q3 must be one that could help people do what?
questions.explanation: Q3's first rule: 'Choose a topic that could help people make decisions' — just like AQI data helps principals and doctors decide.

questions.question: Q3 is in the 'Thinking deeper' level, which is done at your own pace.
questions.explanation: True — the third level is labelled 'Thinking deeper (at your own pace)' and contains the dataset-report task.

questions.question: Q3 required a table with three columns and five rows.
questions.explanation: False — it is the other way round: 5 columns and 3 rows of data.

questions.question: Which table follows Q3's rules?
options: 4 columns, 4 rows, one column is a noise level
5 columns, 3 rows, one column is a cleanliness rating
3 columns, 5 rows, one column is a cleanliness rating
5 columns, 3 rows, no scale column at all
questions.explanation: You need all three: 5 columns, 3 rows AND one scale column. The others swap the numbers, miss the scale, or have the wrong size.

questions.question: Why must one column use a scale?
options: So the table has more words in it
So nobody else can read the table
So readings can be compared fairly
So the table looks more colourful
questions.explanation: A scale (like AQI or a 1–5 cleanliness rating) puts every row on the same measure, so people can compare and decide.

questions.question: Which topic BEST fits Q3's rule 'helps people make decisions'?
options: The planets listed in their order
A list of your favourite cartoons
questions.explanation: Corridor noise data could help the school decide where to put quiet study spaces. Planet order, cartoons and the alphabet don't guide any decision.

questions.question: Students must write one question their dataset CAN answer and one it ___.
questions.explanation: Q3 asks for 'One question your dataset can answer' and 'One question it cannot answer' — knowing the limits of data matters.

questions.question: The Q3 report could be made in a spreadsheet.
questions.explanation: True — Q3 lists 'Canva, Google Slides, or a spreadsheet'.

questions.question: A dataset about corridor noise levels can answer which question?
options: Which city has the cleanest air
Which corridor is noisiest at lunch
Which student is the most clever
questions.explanation: The data is about corridors and noise, so it can compare corridors. It knows nothing about cleverness, kindness or other cities' air.

questions.question: The same corridor-noise dataset CANNOT answer which question?
options: Which time of day is quietest
How noise changes during the week
questions.explanation: A dataset only answers questions about what it measured. Noise readings say nothing about one child's feelings about maths.

questions.question: A dataset can answer any question at all, as long as it has five columns.
questions.explanation: False. Q3 asks for a question the dataset CANNOT answer precisely because every dataset has limits — it only covers what was measured.

questions.question: Which of these is a SCALE column?
options: The date the data was taken
questions.explanation: A scale puts things on a numbered or ranked measure, like a 1-to-5 cleanliness rating. Names, dates and collectors are labels, not scales.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Q3 asked for one ___ and one ___ about making data open.
questions.explanation: The last two writing prompts are 'One benefit of making the data open' and 'One concern about making the data open'.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Which is a BENEFIT of making data open?
options: It can never be copied by anyone
Many people can use it to fix problems
Only its owner can ever read it
It costs a lot to keep it secret
questions.explanation: Open data lets reporters, doctors, governments and researchers all use it — the Delhi story and the WHO study are both benefits of openness.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Which is a CONCERN about making data open?
options: It might let a government make new rules
It might let doctors warn their patients
It might reveal private facts about people
It might help reporters write good stories
questions.explanation: If a dataset includes personal details, opening it could expose people's privacy. The other three are benefits, not concerns.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Select ALL the items that are CONCERNS, not benefits, of open data.
options: Data could be misread or misused
Many people can check the facts
questions.explanation: Privacy risks and misuse are concerns. Faster problem-solving and fact-checking are benefits.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Open data helped the government make clean-air rules, which is a benefit.
questions.explanation: True — better rules that protect people's health are a clear benefit of the data being free and shareable.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: The worksheet says open data has only benefits and no concerns.
questions.explanation: False. Q3 asks for one benefit AND one concern — the worksheet wants you to see both sides.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: A school posts each child's name and home address online as 'open data'. What is the problem?
options: It is stored in a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Names and home addresses are personal. Making them open could put children at risk — this is the kind of concern Q3 asks about.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Open AQI data let the WHO find a world-wide pattern. This is an example of a what?
questions.explanation: Discovering that 99% of people breathe unsafe air — something no single country could find — is a big benefit of open data.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Which is a benefit of open data for the WHO study?
options: Data from 117 countries could be combined
The WHO could sell the data for profit
Only one country's data was needed
questions.explanation: Because governments opened their air data, the WHO could combine readings from 6,000 cities in 117 countries into one database.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Keeping all data secret is always safer and better for everyone.
questions.explanation: False. Secret data would have blocked the Delhi clean-air rules and the WHO finding. Some data needs care (privacy), but 'always secret' loses big benefits.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Why might a city worry before publishing data about its air?
options: It may delete the city's records
It may change the AQI scale used
It may show a problem the city has
It may make the air itself dirtier
questions.explanation: Open data can reveal embarrassing truths, like very poor air. Publishing does not change the air or the scale — it just makes the facts visible.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Which is the fairest view from this chapter?
options: Open data has only benefits and nothing to fear
Open data has only concerns and no benefits
Open data makes no difference to anyone
Open data has big benefits and some real concerns
questions.explanation: The chapter celebrates open data (Delhi rules, WHO finding) but Q3 also asks for a concern. Balanced thinking sees both.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: 'Data that belongs to everyone' lets ordinary people do what?
options: See and use facts for themselves
Print their own money at home
questions.explanation: Open data means the public — not just officials — can look at the numbers and use them, as the reporters did.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: Select ALL the BENEFITS of open data shown in the chapter.
questions.explanation: The Delhi rules and the WHO database are benefits. Letting anyone alter data, or sharing private addresses, would be problems.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: A good way to lower privacy concerns before opening a dataset is to...
options: Keep the dataset only on paper
Add more rows about each person
questions.explanation: Air data has no names, which is why it is safe to open. Taking out personal details lets data be shared without exposing people.

questions.topic: Benefits and Concerns of Open Data
questions.question: The Q3 'concern' prompt teaches students to think about what?
options: How to count the table's rows
How to spell the word dataset
How to colour the table nicely
questions.explanation: Asking for a concern makes you consider who might be hurt or misled if the data is open — responsible data use, not just enthusiasm.

questions.question: In which year did the WHO release its Global Air Quality Database?
questions.explanation: The case study begins: 'In 2022, the World Health Organization (WHO) released its Global Air Quality Database'.

questions.question: What does WHO stand for?
questions.explanation: WHO is the World Health Organization, the global body that published the air quality database.

questions.question: How many cities did the WHO database cover?
questions.explanation: The database covered 'over 6,000 cities across 117 countries'. 117 is the number of countries, not cities.

questions.question: From how many countries did the WHO data come?
questions.explanation: 117 countries. 99 is the percentage of people breathing unsafe air, and 6,000 is the number of cities.

questions.question: Where did every data point in the WHO database come from?
questions.explanation: The text says 'Every data point in it came from open government sources' — governments had made their air data open.

questions.question: What shocking finding did researchers make from the combined database?
options: 99% of people live with air below WHO safety levels
99% of cities measured have perfectly clean air
99% of countries refused to share their data
99% of the world's people live in the 6,000 cities
questions.explanation: The finding: '99% of the world's population lives in places where air quality does not meet WHO safety guidelines.'

questions.question: The WHO database is described as the largest collection of air pollution measurements ever assembled.
questions.explanation: True — the case study calls it 'the largest collection of air pollution measurements ever assembled'.

questions.question: The WHO collected all the air readings itself using its own sensors.
questions.explanation: False. The WHO did not measure the air; every data point came from open government sources that it combined.

questions.question: Why would the 99% finding have been impossible from a single country's data?
options: One country has more than 6,000 cities
One country cannot show the whole world
One country never measures its own air
One country always has very clean air
questions.explanation: A finding about the WORLD's population needs data from many countries. The text says it 'would have been impossible to discover from any single country's data alone'.

questions.question: What made the WHO finding possible?
options: A single scientist visited every city
The WHO guessed the numbers carefully
Thousands of governments opened their data
One rich company bought all the data
questions.explanation: 'This finding was only possible because thousands of governments had made their air data open.'

questions.question: The text says that without openness, no single researcher 'or even a ___' could have done it.
questions.explanation: 'no single researcher — or even a large team — could have collected, verified, and combined data from 6,000 cities across 117 countries.'

questions.question: Select ALL the things the text says would have to be done with data from 6,000 cities.
questions.explanation: The text lists three jobs: collect, verify and combine the data. Selling, hiding or deleting it is the opposite of what open data is for.

questions.question: The WHO finding changed how the world understands air pollution.
questions.explanation: True — the text calls it 'a statistic that changed how the world understands air pollution'.

questions.question: The finding was 'built entirely from information that ___'.
questions.explanation: The last line: 'built entirely from information that belonged to everyone' — tying the case study back to the chapter title.

questions.question: The WHO database covered 117 cities in over 6,000 countries.
questions.explanation: False — the numbers are swapped. It was over 6,000 CITIES in 117 COUNTRIES.

questions.question: Which statement about the WHO database is NOT true?
options: It was released by the WHO in 2022
It was built by one researcher alone
It used open government data sources
questions.explanation: The text stresses that NO single researcher, or even a large team, could have built it alone — it needed thousands of governments' open data.

questions.question: To 'verify' data means to do what?
options: Sort it by the city name
questions.explanation: Verifying means checking the readings are accurate and trustworthy before combining them — a huge job across 6,000 cities.

questions.question: The 99% finding mainly shows that air pollution is...
options: A problem only in very big cities
A problem that has already been solved
A problem nearly everywhere on Earth
questions.explanation: If 99% of all people breathe air below WHO guidelines, dirty air is almost everywhere — not limited to a few places, and certainly not solved.

questions.question: The WHO case study is titled 'One open database. 6,000 cities. The finding that shocked the world.'
questions.explanation: True — that is the heading of the case-study box on the last worksheet page.

questions.question: How does the WHO story connect to the chapter title?
options: Data that belongs to everyone solved a world question
Data that belongs to one company made money
Data that belongs to nobody was thrown away
Data that belongs to the WHO was kept hidden
questions.explanation: Open government data — information belonging to everyone — was combined to answer a question about the whole world's air.

questions.question: The WHO source says billions of people still breathe what kind of air?
questions.explanation: The source title is 'Billions of people still breathe unhealthy air: new WHO data'.

questions.question: Which level comes LAST in the worksheet?
questions.explanation: The order is Laying the tracks (Q1) → Powering up (Q2) → Thinking deeper (Q3). 'Learning is Fun!' is just the closing page.

questions.question: 'Laying the tracks' is the first level of the worksheet.
questions.explanation: True — Q1 (the AQI table) sits under 'Laying the tracks'.

questions.question: Which level is done 'at your own pace'?
questions.explanation: The third level is labelled 'Thinking deeper (at your own pace)' and contains the dataset-report project.

questions.question: How many levels does the worksheet have?
questions.explanation: Three levels: Laying the tracks, Powering up, and Thinking deeper.

questions.question: Select ALL the real level names used in the worksheet.
questions.explanation: The three levels are Laying the tracks, Powering up and Thinking deeper.

questions.question: The worksheet moves from reading a table (Q1) to making your own dataset (Q3). What skill does this build?
questions.explanation: First you read and interpret someone else's AQI data; by Q3 you build and share your own — becoming a maker of open data, not just a user.

questions.question: Which ONE sentence best sums up the whole chapter?
options: Data is useful mainly for making money
Air pollution happens only in Delhi city
Shared data helps people solve real problems
Only governments should collect any data
questions.explanation: That is the worksheet's opening question, answered by the Delhi story and the WHO database. The other sentences contradict the chapter.

questions.question: The chapter's examples were all about water pollution in rivers.
questions.explanation: False. Every example — the AQI table, Delhi smog, the WHO database — is about AIR pollution.

questions.question: Both the Delhi study and the WHO database used data that was...
options: Secret and sold to a few
questions.explanation: The Delhi reporters used free public data; the WHO used open government sources. Openness is what both stories have in common.

questions.question: Which pair shows a 'small local' and a 'big global' use of open data from the chapter?
options: A principal's break-time decision and the WHO 99% finding
The WHO 99% finding and the 117-country database
The Covid-19 pandemic and the 2020 lockdowns
A farmer's crop field and a nearby farmer's field
questions.explanation: A principal keeping pupils indoors is a small local decision; the WHO finding covers the whole world. Both come from the same kind of open air data.

questions.question: In the chapter, data that 'belongs to everyone' means it is...
questions.explanation: Belonging to everyone means nobody is left out — the data is shared, free and open.

questions.question: Select ALL the real-world problems the chapter shows data helping with.
questions.explanation: The two stories are Delhi's smog and the WHO's world air quality database. Mumbai traffic and Chennai floods are not in the chapter.

questions.question: Q1(c)(i) is the only sub-question in Q1 that asks 'why'. What does a 'why' question need?
options: A single number from a table
questions.explanation: Q1(a) and (b) just need a city name read off the table, but 'Why did the AQI improve in 2020?' needs you to explain a cause — the pandemic lockdowns.

questions.question: A student says: 'Only experts should be allowed to see air data.' Which chapter example best disagrees?
options: Farmers burned their crops near Delhi
The AQI scale sits at the top of the table
Reporters used free public data to expose smog
questions.explanation: The Delhi reporters were not government experts, yet with public data they found the cause of the smog and helped change the rules — openness worked.
